name: Cholesky decomposition
seoDesc: Cholesky decomposition: a free math calculator that walks you through 63 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary:
The Cholesky decomposition calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports the result immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer.

That makes it useful for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Cholesky decomposition calculator work?
sections.html:
The Cholesky decomposition calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the matrix size); then you type in the figures it asks for.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cholesky decomposition calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

L₁₁=(A₁, A₂, B₁, B₂, 0, 0)
L₁₂=(A₁, A₂, B₁, B₂, 0, 1)
L₂₁=(A₁, A₂, B₁, B₂, 1, 0)
L₂₂=(A₁, A₂, B₁, B₂, 1, 1)
L₁₁=(A₁, A₂, A₃, B₁, B₂, B₃, C₁, C₂, C₃, 0, 0)
L₁₂=(A₁, A₂, A₃, B₁, B₂, B₃, C₁, C₂, C₃, 0, 1)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Cholesky decomposition calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Cholesky decomposition calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 30 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Cholesky decomposition calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
